Generally speaking, medium and large-scale projects require the preparation of reports, especially for public sector projects such as government departments, hospitals, schools, etc. These reports apply to both renovation projects and new construction projects.

For renovation or upgrade projects, the reports primarily analyze existing issues and proposed solutions, though this is not the main focus. The core purpose of the report is to assist clients in deciding which approach to adopt for advancing the project. The report will detail various options, the pros and cons of each solution, project timelines, budgets, and relevant analyses.

Additionally, the report serves as a basis for the subsequent design phase and is sometimes a required document for regulatory authorities.

However, such cases are relatively rare. There are various types of reports. For renovation or upgrade projects (referred to as Virtual Free), the focus is on analyzing issues in existing projects. These problems are typically raised by clients who cannot resolve them independently. We conduct on-site inspections, produce reports, and then determine the next steps.

For new projects, there are usually Feasibility Study Reports and Basis of Design documents. The Feasibility Study Report primarily assesses the project’s viability. The Basis of Design is established after feasibility approval and before detailed design begins, outlining fundamental content, requirements, and scope.

The Schematic Design Report delves deeper than the Basis of Design and is typically completed at the 20%–30% design stage. For large-scale industrial projects—such as oil & gas or mining—unlike commercial or civil projects, there is a Front End Engineering Design (FEED) phase, applicable to projects with investments exceeding 1 billion RMB. Such reports essentially constitute a comprehensive design package, with a depth at least equivalent to the schematic design phase—or even deeper, akin to preliminary design. For instance, reports for major oil & gas projects previously worked on could span thousands to tens of thousands of pages, far exceeding the scale of typical commercial or civil project reports.

The content is relatively complex and in-depth, with meticulous attention to detail. The primary step in drafting such reports is conducting on-site inspections, followed by communicating with clients to understand their specific requirements.

For renovation or upgrade projects, it is necessary to discuss the specific scope and requirements with the client, including operational issues. Collect all necessary information as conditions and requirements for report preparation.

After entering the information, the next step is to conduct a technical analysis based on our experience and the requirements of current norms and standards. This part should be familiar to everyone, so we won’t go into detail. Once the analysis is complete, the natural next step is drafting the report itself. Later, I’ll show some report samples.

Some reports actually require signatures and seals from professional engineers. These reports typically include charts, tables of contents, specific content, appendices, and photos. As important design documents, these reports also need internal review and final approval by senior engineers.

Normally, these reports are submitted to clients for review. After receiving feedback, we make revisions and resubmit them. For example, BOD (Basis of Design) focuses on technical design aspects, while Feasibility Study involves financial or technical feasibility analysis. Government projects usually require Investment Analysis Reports because government agencies prioritize investment amounts over technical details.

There are various types of these reports, each with different emphases.

Therefore, I can present several case studies for your reference. For instance, this is a project involving generator upgrades for an apartment complex.

The apartment originally did not have a generator as it was not a high-rise building. Now, there is a need to upgrade the generator by replacing it with a higher-capacity unit, which necessitated the preparation of a feasibility study report. The first part of this report serves as the cover page of the final report.

This requires the engineer’s signature and seal.

Below is the table of contents for this report, which includes an overview intended to summarize the overall situation of the facility project and the current status of the system.

Regarding the issues identified on-site, we will conduct a systematic analysis. First, we will describe the current status of the power generation system, including generator specifications and the condition of the electrical room. This is a small-scale project, provided solely for illustrative purposes.

Next is the composite calculation of the single-line diagram. Here are the different option plans: the first option is to maintain the status quo and analyze potential risks; the second option is to perform an upgrade and expansion; the third option is the explanation of the upgraded single-line diagram design scheme.

When formulating this plan, it is necessary to clarify the specific work content, project cost, and timeline.

The advantages and disadvantages as well as risk analysis of this plan are as follows. Although the alternative plan has a higher budget, it delivers better results.

For the same budget item, we analyzed the timeline, pros and cons, and risks. Ultimately, we recommend adopting the upgrade plan, which is the simplest reporting format.

Does anyone have any questions regarding the report content?

Next, I will share the next topic with everyone.

Drawings are one of the most critical technical documents in engineering projects, serving as essential references for construction and mandatory materials for obtaining various permits.

Drawings are one of the most critical technical documents in engineering projects, serving as essential references for construction and mandatory materials for obtaining various permits.

Drawings cover all stages of design, and except for drafting reports, the depth and level of detail in nearly all related drawings are correlated with different phases of the design.

In terms of drafting standards and initial drawing setup, different clients—especially overseas government projects—have stringent specifications. These regulations extend to detailed parameters such as coating selection, color usage, linetype settings, font height, and even explicit requirements for layer naming. Elements like the title block, including scale, must adhere to the standards. Abbreviations, legends, and explanatory text for system diagrams or floor plans must follow established rules and industry conventions.

The aesthetic quality of drawings is equally critical, requiring organized and tidy layouts. Font types and sizes are specified to ensure a cohesive visual presentation. Some government drafting standards documents can span hundreds of pages, containing predefined drawing frame templates that must be strictly followed. Additionally, dedicated programs (e.g., AutoCAD plugins) are provided for compliance checks before final submission, automatically flagging non-compliant details. This reflects a high level of attention to design precision.

A colleague just inquired about the drawing depth and requirements for deliverables at different stages. These questions will be explained in detail later.

Regarding the detailing requirements for Fire Alarm system drawings, apart from floor plans, system diagrams are typically provided by the design team but are not overly detailed. For instance, 18 smoke detectors installed on one floor might be represented by just one or two symbolic notations. However, all types of fire alarm equipment and their interrelationships must be clearly depicted in the drawings.

The Fire Alarm system must include a Fire Alarm Zone Schedule, with zones divided according to Building Code requirements, and fire alarm standards specifying the zoning criteria. Lighting control systems have their own zoning requirements, all of which must be clearly presented in the drawings.

For Security System drafting, the access control section must include a Door Schedule listing the control method for each door and the required access control components. The CCTV system’s Camera Schedule and alarm zones must also be annotated in the drawings.

For mechanical system-related components, such as plumbing, a Motor List is required, detailing the power, voltage, current requirements, and control methods for each HVAC or water supply/drainage equipment. These schedules must be fully documented.

For mechanical system-related components, such as plumbing, a Motor List is required, detailing the power, voltage, current requirements, and control methods for each HVAC or water supply/drainage equipment. These schedules must be fully documented.

An important yet unmentioned aspect of the Fire Alarm system is the Sequence of Operation, which outlines the interlocking requirements during a fire incident. This content must also be reflected in the design.

When designing single line diagrams or electrical equipment rooms, Load Calculation must be performed first. Only after completing the load calculation can the electrical system design proceed.

When designing single line diagrams or electrical equipment rooms, load calculation must be performed first. Only after completing the load calculation can the electrical system design proceed.

After the electrical system design is completed, the electrical equipment can be selected accordingly. Once the equipment selection is finalized, the layout of electrical rooms, generator rooms, UPS, or KCNU can proceed. Therefore, load calculation is the most critical first step. If errors occur in the load calculation, all subsequent work will be incorrect. Hence, the initial load calculation is of utmost importance.

The sequence of operation applies not only to the fire alarm system but also to the load automatic control system and the security system (FABAS security). These details should be reflected in the drawings. Additionally, installation details are included, all of which follow corresponding standards. The above outlines the basic overview of the entire electrical design in the drawings.

Regarding specifications, in North America, small projects may not require a thick book-style specification (book spec); instead, the instructions might simply be attached to the drawings. Domestic projects may adopt similar practices. However, for large-scale projects, preparing a detailed book-style specification is more appropriate. I will elaborate on this later. Here, the focus is on the requirements for different design depths.

Different design phases require the output of different drawings. For example, the Cover Page is needed in all design phases, while the Site Plan is also required throughout most phases. Floor Plans are typically needed only after the 66% design phase, as circuit allocation is usually not assigned at this stage since it is a critical task for the electrical discipline. Floor plans must be provided at the 66%, 99%, and construction drawing phases.

For Enlarged Plans, particularly those for the Electro Room or Generator Room, completion is required in the early stages (e.g., the 33% design phase). This is crucial for determining whether the room dimensions and locations are appropriate, providing a basis for other disciplines such as architecture and plumbing. These details will be further refined and confirmed in subsequent phases.

Single Line Diagrams, including power or low-voltage system diagrams, should be provided starting from the 33% design phase and progressively refined in each subsequent phase.

Panel Schedule is typically completed at the 99% design stage. The various schedules mentioned earlier, including the Lighting Schedule, Mechanical Reformation Schedule, and other schedules, should all be completed by the 99% stage.

Load Calculation needs to be conducted at the very beginning. The Sequence of Operation can be completed at either the 66% or 99% stage. Installation Details are usually added at the 99% stage.

Specifications are generally finalized at the 99% stage, while a table of contents indicating drawing depth is provided at the 66% stage.

Specifications are generally finalized at the 99% stage, while a table of contents indicating drawing depth is provided at the 66% stage.

When determining the depth of design drawings, it is essential to balance three key factors: design quality, engineering budget, and the level of detail in the drawings. If the drawings are overly detailed, they will consume excessive time and may lead to budget overruns; if they are too simplistic, they may fail to meet design quality requirements.

Industrial projects generally have significantly higher design budgets compared to commercial projects due to their larger scale and complexity. For instance, the technical specifications, purchase orders, and related requirements for a single switchgear cabinet can take approximately 40 work hours to complete. In the case of generator projects, while the design cost for a few hundred-kilowatt generator in a civil project may range from 20,000 to 30,000 RMB, industrial projects demand more specialized and detailed design work, with final design costs potentially reaching hundreds of thousands of RMB—nearly equivalent to the cost of the generator itself.

Design fees in North America typically range from 5% to 10%, whereas in China they are only 1% to 3%. The design cycle for North American projects is longer, often lasting one to two years, while in China, even large-scale projects can complete preliminary designs in just one to two months.

These differences lead to distinct outcomes: North American designs are more thorough and comprehensive but progress more slowly, while Asian regions excel in speed. In North America, most issues must be resolved during the design phase; otherwise, immature designs result in frequent changes during construction, making cost control more difficult. For projects of the same scale, the time and cost required for implementation in North America are at least five times higher than in China, a difference closely tied to its stringent process control systems.

In addition, work attitude and work pace are also influencing factors. Next, we will discuss content related to drawings.

Regarding notes in drawings, we typically categorize them into general notes and key notes. General notes apply to universal requirements, while key notes address specific requirements or the scope of work in the drawings. These notes need to be updated in every version of the drawings.

For circuiting in enlarged layouts, due to the substantial workload involved, it is not recommended to conduct detailed design in the early stages. Premature circuit design would lead to increased modification efforts later, so it is generally advised to finalize circuit allocation only during the final drawing issuance phase.

For small projects, overly detailed installation drawings are usually unnecessary. Additionally, contents such as control logic in various schedules and sequences of operation need to be continuously updated and refined across different design phases.

Now let’s talk about how to write this specification document for the Design Management Institute, which serves as a general guideline.

We will proceed with the explanation in the following order. Typically, book specs are primarily applicable to medium to large-scale projects. In the public sector in North America, including government agencies, book specs are required regardless of project size. In the private sector, however, joint specs can be used, where specification requirements are directly annotated on the drawings.

Writing book specs requires deep professional knowledge and broad technical expertise, as they must accurately reflect the specific requirements of a project, particularly those that cannot be clearly expressed in drawings. Additionally, book specs must thoroughly consider the client’s special needs for the project.

It is important to note that consistency must be maintained between the drawings and book specs to avoid contradictions or incoherence. When drafting specifications, relevant industry standards and regulatory requirements must be strictly followed. If conflicts are found between existing specifications and project requirements, timely adjustments should be made to ensure compliance.

In North America, construction specification books (book spec) have specialized templates. The United States has its own template, and Canada has its own, but the two templates are fundamentally similar.

In North America, construction specification books (book spec) have specialized templates. The United States has its own template, and Canada has its own, but the two templates are fundamentally similar.

The American template is developed by the American Institute of Architects (AIA) and is called MasterSpec, while the Canadian version is known as the National Master Specification (NMS). These templates are already quite comprehensive, as will be shown later. They account for various possible scenarios, which is why they are referred to as “Master.” When using them, you only need to select the relevant content based on project requirements or delete unnecessary sections, eliminating the need to write from scratch and saving significant time.

The numbering system for specifications transitioned from five digits to six digits, a change that occurred roughly over a decade ago. Each specification has a numerical code and a corresponding title that describes its specific content. The entire system is divided into 44 Divisions, such as Division 0001, which will be demonstrated in detail later.

These templates require payment to access. In Canada, the template for just the mechanical and electrical sections alone costs around CAD 2,000. The entire template system is updated periodically, but unlike codes that are revised every three or five years, updates may occur every three to five years or sometimes annually. The specific uses of each section will be explained in detail next.

Division01 is General Requirements, which does not target specific technical disciplines but covers general specifications for the entire project, such as project scheduling, meeting organization, and special requirements. It applies to existing renovation or upgrade projects. This section is mainly prepared by the Prime Consultant (i.e., the design general contractor) and requires coordination with other disciplines. It contains less technical content and focuses more on specific management requirements.

The core of our profession lies in specific technical applications. Taking Division 26 as an example, it focuses entirely on the technical specifications of electrical power systems; Division 27 deals with communication systems; while Division 28 primarily covers security systems and related facilities. As for Division 33, its content mainly involves various matters requiring coordination with the electrical department.

Each Division contains multiple Sections, such as distribution panels, generators, lighting systems, etc. All Sections are integrated into a Master document, but specific projects only need to select the applicable parts. This specification package applies to different contractors, typically categorized in North America as electrical contractors (power) and low-voltage contractors. Electrical contractors usually subcontract low-voltage work to specialized contractors.

Special attention must be paid to the division of responsibilities: low-voltage systems such as security and communication wiring, terminations, testing, and commissioning are not handled by electrical contractors. However, electrical contractors are responsible for providing cable routing, conduit installation, grounding, and 120V power support for low-voltage systems. These divisions of labor must be clearly specified in the technical documentation.

For our own stores, in addition to the general front-end specifications 0001 and 02, we also need to understand other relevant specialized content. For example, the architectural discipline covers multiple aspects such as painting, repairs, fireproof coatings, and elevators, all of which are relevant to us. We need to be familiar with these areas and include our requirements in the final proposal.

Regarding the mechanical discipline, it primarily involves plumbing and HVAC systems. This includes Item 23—Electrical Heating, as well as the control of air conditioning systems, which are also relevant to our construction projects. Additionally, Item 25 pertains to the Building Automation System (BAS), which is categorized under the plumbing discipline in North America. Therefore, this section is essentially a specification written for the mechanical discipline.

Items requiring adjustment include project name, date, design phase, etc. The final version must be signed and stamped by an engineer, with a Power Page added. It is recommended to submit all documents as a compressed package.

Implementing a two-stage review or rigorous quality control procedures can significantly improve design quality and reduce errors. High-quality designs not only benefit the project itself but also effectively control construction costs and prevent budget overruns.

If you have a complete set of drawings, it is crucial to ensure consistency among them. If multiple discrepancies exist, contractors will identify and raise numerous questions during bidding, such as asking which drawing is correct. For example, if the single-line diagram specifies 600M while the panel schedule on the switchboard shows 400M, this will cause confusion. Therefore, internal designs must align with each other, including floor plans and system diagrams, panel schedules and single-line diagrams, etc.

The most critical components are the load calculations, single-line diagrams, and main wiring diagrams, especially for fire protection and security systems. Additionally, coordination with other disciplines is extremely important, such as the location and dimensions of the electrical room and substation, as well as the routing of cable trays, large-diameter cables, or conduits. Errors in these aspects during the design phase will have significant impacts during construction.

As consultants, we can provide rough estimates of manpower and working hours, but there is no need for excessive precision since we are not professional budgeting or construction teams. The Communications Authority has extensive experience in construction and strong budgeting capabilities.

In public sector or government projects, budgeting tasks are not necessarily undertaken by private entities or consultants. Depending on the project phase, budget requirements are categorized into four types (A, B, C, D), each with varying levels of precision.

When preparing budgets, the usual approach tends to be relatively rough and lacks high accuracy, as the team is not particularly specialized. Typically, the basis for budgeting includes design documents, drawings, reports, as well as quotations for the electrical equipment and materials to be used. These quotations are usually obtained directly from suppliers or manufacturers.

First, extract the quantity from the equipment documents, then obtain the prices of the equipment and materials from the manufacturer or the industrial and commercial department. At the same time, determine the hourly wages of workers and other expenses. Finally, aggregate all costs to generate the total construction budget.

Often, Excel is used to complete this task, but there is also a tool called the RSMeans Book, which provides data such as material prices and labor costs. Additionally, this system is updated annually based on yearly data.

It is a reference book used for budgeting. There are also specialized software available online, and their calculation results may be more precise.

Is the qualification of a domestically registered electrical engineer recognized internationally, or does the university offer its own certification? Additionally, how can it be converted into an internationally recognized qualification?

In North America, the engineering license systems in the United States and Canada differ. Individual U.S. states have their own licensing systems, similar to driver’s licenses; Canadian provinces also implement comparable systems. In Canada, if an engineer already holds a license in one province, applying for a license in another province typically does not require retaking exams—only submitting an application and paying the fee is needed. For example, applicants with a good record in Ontario can usually obtain a license in British Columbia by completing the formalities.

The requirements for obtaining a license in both the U.S. and Canada include: at least one year of domestic work experience, as well as a bachelor’s degree or higher recognized by the engineering association. Additionally, applicants must have four years of professional work experience, with at least one year completed within Canada. As a result, engineering qualifications obtained in other countries may not be directly transferable in North America.

During the application process, aside from meeting the education and work experience requirements, applicants must also provide recommendation letters from two professional engineers.

Regarding the academic requirements, a foreign graduate degree may meet the criteria, provided it is recognized by the relevant engineering association. Could you introduce the production organization models of foreign design institutes? Are there significant differences compared to domestic design institutes?

There are significant differences between domestic and international design institutes. Most design institutes in China are state-owned enterprises, essentially operating under public ownership. In contrast, foreign design institutes are predominantly privately owned and have different organizational structures. For instance, only a few ultra-large design firms cover all disciplines, while small and medium-sized companies typically specialize in specific fields, such as electrical, plumbing, structural, architectural, site utilities, or even niche areas like energy efficiency or interior design. This stands in stark contrast to the “large and comprehensive” nature of domestic design institutes.

In North America, the construction industry has matured over decades and differs from regions like China, Southeast Asia, or the Middle East, where large-scale resource projects are more common. Here, architectural and structural disciplines hold relatively lower prominence, while MEP (mechanical, electrical, and plumbing) disciplines are far more critical. This is because many office buildings, schools, and hospitals in North America are decades old, and MEP systems require upgrades after 30 years of use, leading to a high volume of retrofit projects. In the North American design industry, MEP is the most in-demand and project-rich discipline.

In such cases, it is advisable to have the architectural discipline act as the overall coordinator, responsible for the holistic design and interdisciplinary coordination.
